questions.q: Why can a more capable model find more creative or subtle ways to exploit specification gaps?
options: Because capability has no relationship to how effectively a system searches for high-reward strategies
Because a more capable system is, among other things, a more effective search process — better at the intended task and at finding gaps in how that task was specified or rewarded
Because more capable models are always given different reward functions
Because capability only affects speed, never strategy discovery
questions.explain: Greater capability generally means a more effective search process across the board, which includes finding subtle exploits of specification or reward gaps, not just finding better intended solutions.

questions.q: What does the lesson mean by calling a weaker model's good behavior a possible "ceiling effect"?
options: The model has reached the maximum possible accuracy on its benchmark
The model appears well-behaved partly because it isn't capable enough to find exploits that exist, rather than because no exploits exist
The model's training was deliberately capped at a fixed number of steps
The model has a hardware limit on memory usage
questions.explain: A weaker model may not exhibit a given specification-gaming behavior simply because it lacks the capability to discover the exploit, not because the underlying gap in the specification has been closed.

questions.q: According to the lesson, do capability and adherence to intended values necessarily improve together as a model scales?
options: Yes, capability improvements always come with proportional alignment improvements
No — capability can scale in ways that don't guarantee intended-value generalization keeps pace, especially in novel situations, though this isn't claimed to happen in every case
No, because capability and values are mathematically identical quantities
Yes, but only for models trained exclusively with supervised learning
questions.explain: The lesson is careful to say this is a reason not to assume alignment improves automatically alongside capability, not an established rule that it always diverges — it's a risk to check for, not a guaranteed outcome.

questions.q: How does the lesson characterize the current state of research on situational awareness and capability scaling?
options: As a fully settled finding that all capable models exhibit strong situational awareness
As an active, open area of empirical research, not a conclusion the field has already reached
As a topic with no ongoing research interest
As something that has been definitively disproven by multiple studies
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly flags situational awareness as an open area of study — a concrete angle researchers use to investigate the broader question, without claiming the field has already reached a settled answer.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect to scalable oversight, covered later in the course?
options: Scalable oversight is presented as a way to avoid training models altogether

If more capable systems can find subtler exploits and don't automatically generalize intended values, the natural follow-up question is how to maintain meaningful supervision once direct human checking no longer scales — which is what scalable oversight addresses
Scalable oversight is unrelated to capability and only concerns hardware scaling
Scalable oversight was fully solved in this chapter and will not be revisited
questions.explain: The chapter's closing argument sets up scalable oversight directly: as capability grows past what humans can easily verify firsthand, the field needs methods for maintaining effective oversight, which is the subject of a later chapter.
